Reference RACI — "Reroute inbound leads" change:

Rules enforced:

  • Exactly one A and at least one R per row.
  • C = consulted (two-way), I = informed (one-way).
  • UAT: Business Owner is Accountable for acceptance; the PM Runs it; Sales SME consult.

Communication plan derived from RACI:

  • Accountable people get decision rights.
  • Responsible people do the work.
  • Consulted people are asked before deciding.
  • Informed people only learn about it after the fact.

Common mistakes:

  • Two A's on one row — creates escalation ping-pong.
  • Listing Inform as Consult because "we want them involved".

Tip: Keep column headers role-based (Sponsor/PM/Business Owner) not name-based — people change, roles persist.
1.3:
Reference interview guide — Warehouse Supervisor (discovery):

Warm-up / context

  1. Walk me through a typical day from when you arrive.
  2. What does your team use to track inbound deliveries today?

Today's process (as-is)

  1. When a truck arrives, who touches the paperwork first — and what happens to it?
  2. How does the office learn that goods are on the dock?
  3. What happens when a delivery is short? Walk me through the last time.

What breaks

  1. What is the single most annoying part of the current process?
  2. If a new starter asked "where does X get entered", what would be confusing?
  3. Where do you lose the most time in a typical day?

Success vision (to-be)

  1. If we fixed ONE thing, which change would make the biggest difference?
  2. If a supervisor could check everything from a phone or one screen, what would you check first?

Closer

  1. Who else should I talk to? Someone who knows the real numbers?
Keep questions open (who/what/why/how), one topic at a time, and let silence do the work.

Common mistakes:

  • Leading questions ("Don't you think the app should...").
  • Yes/no questions that dead-end the conversation.
  • Taking minutes longhand on the spot (transcribe right after, not during).

1.6:
Reference project charter / elevator summary — BrightLogistics:

Current state. Lead-to-dispatch runs across Excel and email; it takes ~2 days for a web inquiry to become a driver's dispatch.

Goal. One CRM where inquiries auto-assign to the right team and dispatch-ready info is one screen away.

In scope. Lead capture, auto-assignment, dispatch list, reporting. Out of scope. Billing changes, driver mobile app.

Stakeholders. Sponsor (CEO), Ops Director, Logistics Mgr, Dispatcher, IT Admin — full RACI in guide 02 / register in 1.4.

Success measure (KPI). Lead-to-dispatch cycle time from 48h → under 4h within 60 days of go-live, with ≥80% of leads auto-assigned without human touch.

Elevator sentence. "Salesforce turns our 2-day manual lead dance into a 4-hour automated flow — one screen, no re-keying, and a dashboard that proves it."

Common mistakes:

  • Success KPIs with no baseline ("improve speed") — always "X → Y by date".
  • Charter written after discovery starts (it should anchor the discovery).

3.2:
Reference BRD outline — "Quarantine" data-cleanup project:

text
1. Background & business goals
   - Why: dirty records drive failed merges and bad reporting.
2. Scope
   - IN: dedupe rules, quarantine workflow, merge-review queue.
   - OUT: historical transformation, external data warehouse.
3. Stakeholders
   - RACI summary (PM accountable, Data SME responsible, review lead consulted).
4. As-is vs to-be
   - As-is: duplicates merged blindly by admins.
   - To-be: system flags, humans review in a quarantine queue.
5. Functional requirements (numbered)
   - R-201 System flags suspected duplicates on email + company.
   - R-202 Flagged records DO NOT auto-merge; they enter the Quarantine queue.
   - R-203 A reviewer can Accept / Reject each suggested merge.
6. Non-functional / data / reporting
   - NFR: quarantine queue loads < 2s even at 50k flagged records.
   - Reporting: merge-acceptance-rate dashboard.
7. Assumptions, dependencies, open questions
   - Assumption: duplication field rules owned by the Data team.
   - Open Q: should admins bypass the queue? (pending sponsor)

Common mistakes:

  • Skipping explicit out-of-scope — that's the #1 scope-creep leak.
  • Writing requirements with buzzwords ("enhance", "robust") instead of behavior.

Key modeling decisions:

  • A Session links BOTH a Student and a Tutor (two lookups resolve the many-to-many via an event).
  • Review is Master-Detail on Session — it cannot exist without its session.
  • Payment references Student; Session link is optional (a family may pay without a session line).

  • Turning every phrase ("favorite tutor") into a field instead of a relationship.
4.2:
Reference Lookup vs Master-Detail decisions:

RelationshipChoiceJustification
Student → SessionLookupA student can exist with zero sessions (prospect).
Tutor → SessionLookupA tutor exists before assignment; sessions reschedule freely.
Session → ReviewMaster-DetailA review has no life without its session; cleanest delete cascade.
Student → PaymentLookupPayments exist before sessions (deposits); no delete cascade on financial data.

Why not MD for Payment? MD forces shared ownership and roll-up summaries — financial data usually wants looser grouping.

When you'd flip to Master-Detail:

  • If a REVIEW-ONLY-child rule is strict (no orphan reviews), MD is correct and you get a Rating roll-up for free.

Common mistakes:

  • Choosing MD "because it's stronger" — cascade delete and shared ownership are real consequences.

5.2:
GWT acceptance criteria — "Student reschedules a session within 6 hours of its start":

gherkin
Scenario: Student reschedules in time (happy path)
  Given a session is Scheduled to start in 12 hours
  And the student is the session's assigned learner
  When the student picks a new preferred time
  Then the session is re-scheduled to the new time
  And the previous time slot is released
  And the tutor receives a reschedule notification

Scenario: Reschedule is too late (fail case)
  Given a session is Scheduled to start in 2 hours
  When the student submits a reschedule request
  Then the request is rejected
  And the session remains at the original time
  And the student is told they missed the 6-hour cut-off

Scenario: The new time conflicts with the tutor (edge case)
  Given the student's preferred time overlaps a tutor busy slot
  When the student submits a reschedule request
  Then the system returns 3 alternative free slots within 7 days
  And the student must pick one before the change saves

Why three scenarios: happy path proves the main value; the fail case protects the 6h cut-off rule; the edge case forces a conflict-resolution decision the developer shouldn't guess.

Common mistakes:

  • Writing criteria without the actor + trigger context ("the system reschedules" — who, when, why?).
  • Stopping at happy path — every rule needs its fail path.

8.1:
UAT plan — "Duplicate lead suppression" mini-feature:

  • Scope: quarantine queue, review accept/reject, merge action (in). Periodic cleanup job (out).
  • Participants: 2 data reviewers (business), 1 data SME, BA (moderator), dev (support on-call).
  • Environment: full-copy sandbox, anonymized records matching prod volumes.

  • Scenarios (2+):

    1. Submit a web lead that duplicates an existing email → verify it lands in quarantine, NOT the list.
    2. Review a queue item → Accept merges master + child; Reject releases the record untouched.
  • Schedule: Day 1-2 test execution (2 daily cycles), Day 3 defect fix + retest, Day 4 sign-off gate.

  • Exit criteria (measurable):

    • 100% of scripted scenarios executed;
    • ≥ 95% steps passed without workaround;
    • 0 open Severity 1 defects; Sev-2 must have a workaround and a fix date;
    • All captured defects retested and closed or deferred with owner.
  • Sign-off: business owner signs the UAT sign-off record; gate = go/no-go meeting.

Common mistakes:

  • Exit criteria without numbers — "all tests pass" is not a gate.

60-second BA elevator pitch (≤140 words):

"When a company installs Salesforce, the software is easy — the messy part is deciding what to build and who it's for. I'm the person who makes that decision crisp.

I spend the first weeks in the business: shadowing dispatchers, mapping the sticky-notes on the wall, and turning 'it's all manual' into numbered, testable requirements. On my last engagement I cut lead-to-dispatch from 48 hours to under 4 — the sponsor saw it on a live dashboard, and UAT wrapped in five days because every story had measurable acceptance criteria.

What I hand you at the end isn't a pile of documents — it's a build team that knows exactly what to build, and a user base that's already been listened to. That's why projects I BA for ship on time and get adopted."

Why it works: opens with a business outcome, names the method (shadowing → testable requirements), closes with a measurable win and a promise to the build team + users.

Common mistakes:

  • Listing tools/terms instead of outcomes ("I do RFCs, BRDs, SARs, RACIs...").

3. Three user stories + acceptance criteria

As a web customer, I want my inquiry to create a lead instantly, so that I'm not stuck waiting for an email reply. Given I submit a valid web form, When the submission arrives, Then a Lead is created within 60s (GWT: happy + missing-email error case).
As a dispatcher, I want to see only my territory's leads, so that I never re-sort the pile. Given leads exist in two states, When I open my queue, Then only leads matching my territory are listed (edge: unassigned = visible to supervisor only).
As the sales manager, I want a source-to-close report, so that I can shift budget to winning channels. Given 90 days of closed data, When I open the report, Then conversion % is correct per source to two decimals (fail: filter excludes deleted).

text
1. Background & goals

MP6:
Backlog scoring model — value × urgency − effort − risk:

Model definition (decided first):

  • Value 0-10 (business worth if shipped), Urgency 0-10 (time pressure), Effort 1-5, Risk 1-5.
  • Score = (Value × Urgency) − (Effort + Risk).

Scored table (6 stories): | Story | Value | Urgency | Effort | Risk | Score | Rank | |-------|------:|--------:|-------:|-----:|------:|-----:| | Auto-assign leads | 9 | 10 | 4 | 2 | 84 | 1 | | Quarantine duplicates | 8 | 8 | 3 | 3 | 58 | 2 | | Source-to-close report | 7 | 7 | 2 | 2 | 53 | 3 | | Email notifications | 6 | 5 | 1 | 1 | 32 | 4 | | French translation | 3 | 4 | 2 | 2 | 8 | 5 | | Driver mobile portal | 4 | 2 | 5 | 4 | -1 | 6 |

Defense of rank #1:

  • Auto-assign is the highest product of value × urgency (90), races the fastest to a visible win, and its effort (4) is reliable because it mirrors an existing proven routing implementation — the only real risk is business-rule drift, which we retired via a decision log. Every other story scores lower on at least one of the two multiplier terms and therefore stays later.

Success check: any stakeholder can re-run the model without you standing over their shoulder.
MP7:
UAT cycle — "Duplicate lead suppression":

UAT plan (excerpt):

  • Scope: quarantine queue, review accept/reject. Exit criteria: 100% scenarios executed; ≥95% steps passed clean; 0 Sev-1 open; all defects retested.

4 test cases: | ID | Steps | Expected | |----|-------|----------| | TC-1 | Submit a lead duplicating an existing email | Lead enters Quarantine, not the main list | | TC-2 | Open queue, Accept a merge | Master absorbs child; child archived; logging visible | | TC-3 | Open queue, Reject a merge | Record released untouched; history notes reject reason | | TC-4 | Reviewer role without queue access opens the tab | Tab empty with permission notice (no error) |

One defect + retest note:

DEF-01 (Sev-2): Accepting two merges in a row on the same pair applies the second without re-verification. → Fixed via re-check of master status. Retest: TC-2 run twice; PASSED with status lock visible.

Sign-off record (go/no-go): Exit criteria met → Go. Decision logged with the two Sev-2 workarounds and future-dates.

Success check: the gate decision is backed by criteria, not memory.
